info.title: Zebra Handheld RFID Reader (RFD40/RFD90) IoT Connector API
info.description:
Standardized MQTT API contract for the Zebra IoT Connector (IoTC) on RFD40 and RFD90 connected handheld RFID readers, over Wi-Fi and Ethernet.

This document is the AsyncAPI 3.0.0 description of the IoTC MQTT interface. It is authored as AsyncAPI because the transport is asynchronous MQTT publish/subscribe: messages travel on bi-directional topic hierarchies with per-message QoS and RETAIN semantics, correlation is by an application-level `requestId` echoed on a shared topic, and the reader emits unsolicited events that no request/response model can express.

**Source of truth.** Every message payload -- its fields, field order, types, enums, constraints, required members, descriptions and examples -- is taken from the IoT Connector API definition, `openapi.json`, and the schema files it references (`commands/`, `response/`, `events/` and `refrence/`). The response codes are taken from the response-code catalogue dated 2026-09-21. Transport behaviour that the API definition does not describe -- topics, QoS, RETAIN, delivery and correlation -- is documented on the servers, channels and operations of this document.

**Reading the contract.** Direction is stated from the reader's point of view: `receive` means the reader subscribes and the cloud publishes; `send` means the reader publishes. Every command operation declares its `reply`, so the channel a response arrives on is part of the contract rather than a convention.

## How this document maps to the API definition

| `openapi.json` | This document |
| --- | --- |
| Request body of `/<command>` (tags `Control`, `Device Management`) | Payload of the `<command>` command message, consumed by operation `receive_<command>` |
| `200` response of `/<command>` | Payload of the reply message, declared as the `reply` of `receive_<command>` |
| `/alerts`, `/dataEVT`, `/heartBeatEVT`, `/mqttConnEVT` (tag `Events`) | Payloads of `alertEvent`, `dataEvent`, `heartBeatEvent` and `epConnectionEvent` |
| Named examples of a request or response | The message's `examples`, with the same names, descriptions, payloads and order |

Each payload schema is written out in full -- every `$ref` of the API definition is resolved in place and no composition keyword is added -- so the schema of a message always shows every field the message can carry, whichever example is selected. The one composition keyword left is the `anyOf` the API definition itself declares for `heartBeatEvent.data`. Field order is the order of the API definition. Payload schemas use the default AsyncAPI schema format, a superset of JSON Schema Draft 07; the API definition's `example` values appear as single-item `examples` arrays. The source file of each payload is named at the end of its message description.

## Quickstart

Everything below is part of the contract. If you read only this section you can send a command and understand the reply.

### 1. The topic model

Every topic is three segments:

```text
{tenantId} / <channel topic> / {deviceSerialNumber}
     |              |                  |
     |              |                  +-- the reader appends this (its own serial)
     |              +-- the only part you configure
     +-- the reader prepends this
```

**You configure only the middle segment**, per endpoint, through `mqttParams.publishTopics[].topic` and `mqttParams.subscribeTopics[].topic`. Writing the tenant identifier or the serial number into a configured value produces a doubled topic that nothing subscribes to -- this is the single most common configuration mistake with this API. The three segments are specified in full under `components.parameters`.

### 2. Connect

MQTT **3.1.1** over TCP. Use port **8883 with TLS** (`protocol: MQTT_TLS`) on any untrusted network; 1883 is plaintext and sends your credentials in the clear inside the CONNECT packet. The username and password go in the **MQTT CONNECT packet**, not in any payload, and they are the ones configured through `config_endpoint` as `mqttParams.username` and `mqttParams.password`. See `servers.iotcBroker` for the host and port variables, the keep-alive, the clean-session flag and the Last-Will registration.

### 3. Subscribe BEFORE you publish

This ordering is not a style preference. Replies and alerts are **not retained**, so anything published before your subscription is active is lost and will not be redelivered. Three commands -- `set_os`, `install_certificate` and `reboot` -- reply with an acknowledgement (code 1, `Command payload is accepted`) and report their real outcome later on the event channel, so a client that subscribes after publishing can miss the outcome entirely.

Subscribe to the response topic for your tenant and reader:

```text
acme/MGMT/clients/resp/RFD40-211545201D0034
```

### 4. Publish a command, and correlate the reply

Choose a fresh `requestId` for every request. The reader echoes it back verbatim, and it is the **only** thing pairing a reply with its request -- commands and replies share one topic pair, and replies arrive out of order and interleaved with events.

```json
{
  "command": "get_status",
  "requestId": "abc123"
}
```

The reply, on the response topic:

```json
{
  "command": "get_status",
  "requestId": "abc123",
  "apiVersion": "V1.21",
  "deviceStatus": {
    "powerSource": "USB",
    "radioActivity": "INACTIVE",
    "radioConnection": "DISCONNECTED",
    "systemTime": "2026-06-15T09:26:00.443Z"
  },
  "response": {
    "code": 0,
    "description": "Success"
  }
}
```

### 5. Branch on the code, never on the text

A reply's `response` object has two required members, `code` and `description`; `response` itself is required on every reply except `set_os`, whose schema leaves it optional. Treat a reply as successful when `response.code` is `0`. Code `1` is an acknowledgement, not a success: the work is still running.

**Never parse `response.description`.** It is human-readable text that may change between firmware builds. `response.code` is the normative outcome; the full catalogue, with the firmware constant, the cause and the recommended action for every code, is under **Response codes** below, and the subset that applies to one command is on that command's operation.

**Retry only when the recommended action names a condition that can change without changing your request** -- wait, stop the inventory, charge the device, free up flash. Treat every other code as terminal until the request itself changes. The machine-readable catalogue in `info.x-iotc-response-codes` carries a `retryable` marker derived from exactly that rule.

### 6. What you do not get

**There is no timeout.** Firmware specifies none, for any command; reply latency depends on network and device conditions. Choose your own patience budget.

**Repeats are not suppressed.** The reader keeps no request history: every copy that arrives is acted on, and for a configuration command the last one to arrive wins. A command whose work is already running is refused with a status code that says so. Each command operation carries an `x-iotc-idempotent` marker and states in prose whether repeating it is safe.

## Response codes

The values of `response.code`, from the IoT Connector response-code catalogue dated 2026-09-21. **Commands** lists the commands the catalogue scopes a code to; `all` means the code may accompany the reply to any command.

| Code | Meaning | Constant | Commands | Cause | Recommended action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Success | `IOT_STATUS_SUCCESS` | all | Command executed successfully | No action required |
| 1 | Command payload is accepted | `IOT_STATUS_CMD_PAYLOAD_ACCEPTED` | `set_os`, `reboot`, `install_certificate` | The device accepted the payload and is processing it asynchronously | Wait for a follow-up event or poll status to confirm completion |
| 2 | Invalid payload | `IOT_ERROR_INVALID_PAYLOAD` | `set_wifi`, `delete_wifi_profile` | The JSON payload is malformed or contains invalid field values | Validate the payload against the command schema and correct any errors |
| 3 | Not able to retrieve information | `IOT_ERROR_INFO_NOT_AVAILABLE` | `get_status` `get_endpoint_config`, `get_wifi`, `get_eth`, `get_current_region`, `get_installed_certificates`, `get_operating_mode`, `get_post_filter` | The device could not gather the requested information at this time | Retry the command after a short delay; if persistent, reboot the device |
| 4 | Firmware update in progress | `IOT_STATUS_FW_UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS` | `set_os` | A firmware update is already running on the device | Wait for the current update to complete before sending another set_os command |
| 5 | Can't reboot device, inventory in progress | `IOT_ERROR_IN_REBOOT_INVENTORY_IN_PROGRESS` | `reboot` | An RFID inventory operation is currently active | Stop the inventory with control_operation before rebooting |
| 6 | Region is not configured | `IOT_STATUS_REGION_NOT_CONFIGURED` | `cloud_connect` | No regulatory region has been set on the device | Configure the region before attempting to connect |
| 7 | Interface is not available | `IOT_ERROR_INTERFACE_NOT_AVAILABLE` | `cloud_connect` | The requested network interface is not present or not enabled | Verify the device has the required network interface and that it is enabled |
| 8 | Insufficient flash size | `IOT_ERROR_LOW_FLASH_SIZE` | `set_os` | Not enough free flash storage to download the firmware file | Free up flash space or use a smaller firmware package |
| 9 | File not found | `IOT_STATUS_FILE_NOT_FOUND` | `install_certificate`, `delete_certificate`, `get_installed_certificates`, `set_os` | The specified file or certificate could not be found on the device or server | Verify the file path or URL is correct and the file exists |
| 10 | Configuration already exists | `IOT_ERROR_CONFIG_ALREADY_EXIST` | `config_endpoint` | An endpoint or configuration with the same name already exists | Delete the existing configuration first or use a different name |
| 11 | Inventory in progress | `IOT_ERROR_INVENTORY_IN_PROGRESS` | `control_operation`, `set_operating_mode` | An RFID inventory operation is currently running | Stop the current inventory before starting a new operation or changing the mode |
| 12 | No Radio Operation in Progress | `IOT_ERROR_NO_RADIO_OP_IN_PROGRESS` | `control_operation` | A stop command was sent but no radio operation is currently active | No action required — the radio is already idle |
| 13 | Firmware update Failed | `IOT_ERROR_FW_UPDATE_FAIL` | `set_os` | The firmware download or installation failed | Check the firmware URL, network connectivity, and retry the update |
| 14 | Battery is low, Cannot update firmware | `IOT_ERROR_FW_UPDATE_FAIL_LOW_BATTERY` | `set_os` | Battery charge is too low to safely perform a firmware update | Charge the device or connect to external power before retrying |
| 15 | WIFI Error - SSID not found | `IOT_ERROR_SSID_NOT_FOUND` | `set_wifi`, `delete_wifi_profile` | The specified Wi-Fi SSID does not exist in saved profiles | Verify the SSID name is correct and that the profile has been saved |
| 16 | WIFI Error - Cannot delete active SSID | `IOT_ERROR_DELETE_ACTIVE_SSID` | `delete_wifi_profile` | The Wi-Fi profile being deleted is the currently connected network | Disconnect from the network or connect to a different SSID before deleting |
| 17 | WIFI Error - SSID missed | `IOT_ERROR_SSID_MISSED` | `set_wifi`, `delete_wifi_profile` | The required SSID field is missing from the payload | Include the SSID field in the command payload |
| 18 | WIFI Error - SSID already exist | `IOT_ERROR_SSID_ALREADY_EXIST` | `set_wifi` | A Wi-Fi profile with this SSID is already saved on the device | Delete the existing profile first or update it instead of creating a new one |
| 19 | WIFI Error - SSID count overflow | `IOT_ERROR_SSID_LIMIT_OVERFLOW` | `set_wifi` | The maximum number of saved Wi-Fi profiles has been reached | Delete an unused Wi-Fi profile before adding a new one |
| 20 | Wifi is not supported | `IOT_ERROR_WIFI_INTER_NOT_SUPPORTED` | `set_wifi` | The device hardware does not have a Wi-Fi interface | Use Ethernet or another supported interface for network connectivity |
| 21 | Certificate not found | `IOT_ERROR_CERT_NOT_FOUND` | `delete_certificate`, `get_installed_certificates`, `install_certificate` | The specified certificate is not installed on the device | Verify the certificate name and install it using install_certificate if needed |
| 22 | Advanced configuration not set | `IOT_CTRL_ADVANCED_PROFILE_NOT_SET` | `set_operating_mode` | The operating mode requires an advanced profile that has not been configured | Configure the advanced profile settings before setting the operating mode |
| 23 | Invalid enum value | `IOT_ERROR_INVALID_ENUM` | `config_endpoint` `set_wifi`, `install_certificate`, `control_operation`, `set_operating_mode`, `set_post_filter` | A field value does not match any of the allowed enum options | Check the schema for allowed values and correct the field |
| 24 | Max 32 prefilters limit exceeded | `IOT_ERROR_PREFILTERS_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` | `set_operating_mode` | More than 32 prefilter rules were specified | Reduce the number of prefilter rules to 32 or fewer |
| 25 | Max 3 publish topics exceeded | `IOT_ERROR_PUBLISH_TOPICS_EXCEEDED` | `config_endpoint` | More than 3 publish topics were specified in the endpoint configuration | Reduce the number of publish topics to 3 or fewer |
| 26 | Max 1 subscribe topic exceeded | `IOT_ERROR_SUBSCRIBE_TOPIC_EXCEEDED` | `config_endpoint` | More than 1 subscribe topic was specified in the endpoint configuration | Use only 1 subscribe topic per endpoint |
| 27 | Invalid tenant ID length | `IOT_ERROR_INVALID_TENANTID_LENGTH` | `config_endpoint` | The tenant ID exceeds the maximum allowed character length | Shorten the tenant ID to within the allowed limit |
| 28 | Tag match pattern length exceeded | `IOT_ERROR_TAG_MATCH_PATTERN_LENGTH_EXCEEDED` | `set_operating_mode` | The tag match pattern string exceeds the maximum allowed length | Shorten the tag match pattern to within the allowed limit |
| 29 | Url missing for HTTP source | `IOT_ERROR_URL_MISSING` | `install_certificate` | The URL for the HTTP source is missing | Provide a valid URL for the HTTP source |
| 30 | Certificate content missing for direct source | `IOT_ERROR_CERT_CONTENT_MISSING` | `install_certificate` | The certificate content is missing for the direct source | Provide the required certificate content for the direct source |
| 31 | Max write length exceeded | `IOT_ERROR_MAX_WRITE_LENGTH_EXCEEDED` | `set_operating_mode` | The maximum write length for the certificate has been exceeded | Ensure the certificate size is within the allowed limit. |
| 32 | Write data length mismatch | `IOT_ERROR_WRITE_DATA_LENGTH_MISMATCH` | `set_operating_mode` | The length of the data being written does not match the expected length | Ensure the data length matches the length value added on payload if field given. |
| 33 | Endpoint already configured | `IOT_ERROR_ENDPOINT_ALREADY_CONFIGURED` | `config_endpoint` | An endpoint with the same configuration already exists on the device | Delete the existing endpoint configuration first or modify it instead of creating a new one |
| 34 | Certificate base64 decode failed | `IOT_ERROR_CERT_BASE64_DECODE_FAILED` | `install_certificate` | The base64 encoded certificate content could not be decoded | Ensure the certificate content is correctly base64 encoded and try again |
| 35 | Can't modify an active endpoint | `IOT_ERROR_CANT_MODIFY_ACTIVE_ENDPOINT` | `config_endpoint` | An attempt was made to modify an endpoint that is currently active | Deactivate the endpoint before making modifications |
| 36 | Missing client key or client certificate | `IOT_MISSING_CLIENT_KEY_OR_CERT` | `install_certificate` | When client certificate and its client key are not sent together for installation | Always install client certificate with its key |
| 37 | Invalid verification type for MQTT TLS | `IOT_INVALID_MQTT_TLS_VERIFICATION_TYPE` | `config_endpoint` | The verification type specified for MQTT TLS is can't be NONE | Specify a valid verification type for MQTT TLS such as verify host, verify peer or verify host and peer |
| 101 | Default error | -- | all | This is an error code for unknown or unhandled errors. It is a catch-all for any error that does not have a specific code assigned. | Investigate the error and take appropriate action based on the context. |

Codes 6 and 7 are scoped by the catalogue only to `cloud_connect`, which is not a command of this API, so no command documented here returns them. The catalogue spells one command `get_installed_certificate`; that is the `get_installed_certificates` command documented here. Code 101 has no firmware constant.

## About the values in the examples

The examples are reproduced verbatim from `openapi.json`, field for field and in the same key order. The host names, IP addresses, serial numbers, passwords, certificate bodies and keys in them are sample values from the API definition: treat none of them as working material, and never reuse a sample credential or key in a deployment.

x-iotc-response-codes.wildcardMeaning: A `commands` value of `*` in the catalogue means the code may accompany the reply to any command. Those codes are reported here as `universal: true` with an empty `commands` list.
x-iotc-response-codes.retryDerivation: `retryable` is derived mechanically from `recommendedAction`, never hand-assigned. In order: the acceptance ack (code 1) is `not-applicable`, because an acknowledgement is not an outcome; an action beginning "no action required" is `not-applicable`; an action naming a condition that can change without changing the request (wait, retry, stop the inventory, charge the device, free up space, delete an unused profile) is `yes`; an action naming something about the request itself that must be different (verify, correct, provide, shorten, configure, install) is `no`. An entry matching neither list fails the build rather than defaulting, so a future code cannot be silently classified.

iotcBroker.title: IoTC MQTT broker
iotcBroker.summary: The MQTT broker the reader connects to, as configured by config_endpoint.
iotcBroker.description: The broker endpoint is not fixed by this API -- it is configured on the device through `config_endpoint`, which is why host and port are server variables rather than literals. `protocolVersion` is `3.1.1`; the reader reports the negotiated version in the `mqttVersion` field of its connection-state message. The reader supports QoS 0 and 1. The QoS of each topic is set in its `mqttParams.publishTopics[]` or `mqttParams.subscribeTopics[]` entry when the endpoint is configured.

brokerHost.description: Broker hostname or IP address, taken from the endpoint configuration `url`. **There is no default**, deliberately: the broker is deployment specific and this contract has no way to know yours. An earlier revision defaulted this to a development-machine hostname, which would silently point a generated client at nothing.

brokerPort.description: Broker TCP port. 1883 is plaintext MQTT and 8883 is MQTT over TLS; the API definition's examples use 1883 with `protocol: MQTT` and 8883 with `protocol: MQTT_TLS`.

lastWill.message: The DISCONNECTED form of epConnectionEvent, registered with the broker at CONNECT time and published by the broker if the reader disconnects ungracefully. Because it is registered before the disconnect happens it cannot carry a live timestamp, which is the one documented exception to the rule that every event carries one. A clean DISCONNECT suppresses it, so its arrival specifically indicates an unexpected loss of the reader.

command.title: Command channel
command.summary: Commands the application publishes and the reader consumes.
command.description:
Inbound command channel. The RFD40/RFD90 **subscribes** here; your application **publishes** to it.

Note the naming: this segment is configured in the endpoint's `subscribeTopics`, never in `publishTopics`, because both arrays are named from the reader's point of view. An endpoint may carry at most **one** subscribe topic; exceeding that returns status code 26.

QoS 1 (at-least-once): a lost command is indistinguishable from one the device declined to answer. At-least-once means a command may arrive twice, and **the reader does not suppress the repeat**. There is no `requestId` history and no suppression window: every copy that arrives is executed. For a configuration command the last one to arrive is the one that takes effect; for a command whose work is already running, the second copy is refused with the status code for that condition -- a repeated `set_os` returns 4 `Firmware update in progress`, and a repeated `set_wifi` CREATE returns 18 `WIFI Error - SSID already exist`. Consult the per-command `x-iotc-idempotent` marker and the prose beside it before retrying anything.

RETAIN is false: a retained command would be re-delivered and re-executed on every reconnect, which for `reboot` or `set_os` would be actively harmful.

externalDocs.description: Reference documentation for the `command` channel and its topic model.

response.title: Response channel
response.description:
Outbound response channel. The reader publishes every command reply here, echoing the originating `requestId`.

Replies arrive **out of order and interleaved with events**, so a client must correlate on `requestId` rather than rely on ordering.

QoS 1: a lost reply leaves the caller unable to tell success from failure. RETAIN is false -- a retained reply would reach a future subscriber as though it answered a request that subscriber never sent.

externalDocs.description: Reference documentation for the `response` channel and its topic model.

event.title: Event and alert channel
event.summary: Unsolicited alerts and notifications the reader publishes.
event.description:
Outbound asynchronous event channel: alerts and notifications that answer no command. Which event types are emitted is controlled by `config_events`.

QoS is **per message**, not uniform across the channel. `alertEvent` travels at QoS 1, because losing an alert is operationally serious; `heartBeatEvent` travels at QoS 0, because a heartbeat is redundant by definition and losing one is harmless. Each is declared on its own operation.

RETAIN is false: an alert describes an instant, and a retained alert would be replayed to new subscribers as current long after the condition cleared.

Events carry no common field naming the event kind, so subscribers must discriminate structurally on the required property set: `alertEvent` requires `type`, `timestamp`, `state`, `id` and `priority`; `heartBeatEvent` requires `eventName`, `timestamp` and `eventNumber`.

externalDocs.description: Reference documentation for the `event` channel and its topic model.

rfidData.title: Shared-endpoint tag data and connection state
rfidData.summary: Tag data routed to a shared management or control endpoint, plus connection-state events.
rfidData.description:
Outbound channel on a **shared** endpoint -- one whose base segment is `MGMT`, `CTRL` or similar, rather than a dedicated data endpoint. It carries two unrelated kinds of message, which is why QoS and RETAIN are declared per operation:

- **Tag data** (`dataEvent`), when inventory output is routed to a shared endpoint instead of a dedicated data channel. QoS is configurable and defaults to 0.
- **Connection state** (`epConnectionEvent`), the birth and Last-Will messages. Every active endpoint emits its own on **its own** `rfid` topic, at QoS 0. Its RETAIN flag is declared on `send_epConnectionEvent` (`true`), so a subscriber that connects after a transition is handed the last connection state by the broker.

Tag data on this channel is always published with RETAIN false.

For high-rate inventory prefer a dedicated data endpoint -- see `data1Event` and `data2Event`.

externalDocs.description: Reference documentation for the `rfidData` channel and its topic model.

data1Event.title: Dedicated tag-data channel 1
data1Event.summary: First dedicated data-plane channel for tag-read output.
data1Event.description:
Outbound tag-data stream on the **first** dedicated data channel, carried by an endpoint configured with `epType: "DATA1"`.

Receiving `dataEvent` here requires an **active data endpoint**: create one with `config_endpoint` at `epType: "DATA1"` and `activate: true`. Without it no tag data arrives on this address, whatever the radio is doing -- which is the single most common reason an integrator sees an inventory running and no data.

The reader's default endpoint configurations use 0, because inventory produces reads faster than an acknowledged flow can confirm them; an application that needs guaranteed capture must reconcile against `inventoryStatus` rather than assume the stream is complete. send_dataEvent_shared.title: send_dataEvent_shared
send_dataEvent_shared.summary: Stream tag-read data on a shared management or control endpoint.
send_dataEvent_shared.description:
The reader publishes tag and barcode read data to `{tenantId}/MGMT/clients/rfid/{deviceSerialNumber}` when inventory output is routed to a **shared** endpoint rather than to a dedicated data endpoint.

This is the fallback placement, not the preferred one: sharing the management or control endpoint puts high-rate tag traffic on the same topic tree as connection-state events. radioStartConditions.title: radioStartConditions
radioStartConditions.description:
Configures how and at what time intervals inventory of tags should be started. 

If this configuration is absent, by default radio will immediately begin inventorying tags upon receiving a "start" command.

trigger.description: Represents the trigger configuration to start the inventory operation.  - `PRESSED`: Inventory starts when the trigger is pressed. - `RELEASED`: Inventory starts when the trigger is released. - `IMMEDIATE`: Inventory starts immediately without requiring a trigger action.

startDelay.description: Specifies the delay (in milliseconds) before starting the inventory operation.  This delay applies to any trigger configuration when set to a value greater than 0.  For example, if set to 3000 milliseconds, the inventory will start 3 seconds after the trigger action.

repeat.description: Determines whether the inventory operation can be repeated using the trigger.  If enabled, pressing the trigger will start reading tags, and releasing it will stop the read operation (not abort).  Pressing the trigger again will restart the inventory operation. If disabled, pressing the trigger after stopping the inventory will not restart the operation.

radioStopConditions.title: radioStopConditions
radioStopConditions.description:

If this configuration is absent, the radio will continue inventorying tags until a "stop" command is issued.

trigger.description: Represents the trigger configuration to stop the inventory operation.  - `PRESSED`: Inventory stops when the trigger is pressed. - `RELEASED`: Inventory stops when the trigger is released. - `IMMEDIATE`: Inventory stops immediately without requiring a trigger action.

stopTimeout.description: Specifies the duration (in milliseconds) after which the inventory operation will stop.

query.title: query
query.description: Configures the query parameters for inventory operations including session, target, and tag population to optimize tag selection and reading.

session.description: Session field (see EPC Gen2 Spec). Determines the session used for inventory operations.  Sessions are used to manage tag states and collisions during inventory.  SESSION_0 is typically used for single inventory rounds, while SESSION_1, SESSION_2, and SESSION_3  are used for multi-round inventories with varying persistence levels.

slFlag.description: SL (Select) flag field (see EPC Gen2 Spec). Indicates the SL (Select) flag used to filter tags.  'ALL' selects all tags regardless of SL flag state.  'ASSERTED' selects only tags with an asserted SL flag, while 'DEASSERTED' selects tags with a deasserted SL flag.

tagPopulation.description: Estimates tag count to optimize reading. This value helps the reader adjust its settings  (e.g., Q parameter) to improve inventory performance for the expected number of tags in the field.

select.description:
Configures the pre-filtering of tags during inventory operations. 
This allows for selective reading of tags based on specific criteria, optimizing inventory performance.
Supports up to 32 select filters.

items.title: select
items.description: Defines the select pre-filter configuration for filtering tags before inventory.

enable.description: Used to enable and disable the pre-filter. Set to true to enable the pre-filter,  allowing the reader to apply specific filtering criteria to tags before inventory operations.

The value must be a hex string (only values 0-9, a-f or A-F) and must have an even number of characters, max 64 characters.  This is used to filter tags based on specific data stored in their memory(see EPC Gen2 Spec).

memoryBank.description: Membank field (see EPC Gen2 Spec). Specifies the memory bank to be accessed for filtering.

offset.description: Indicates the starting bit position within the specified memory bank where the tagPattern will be applied for matching(see EPC Gen2 Spec).

action.description: Defines how to set SL/invnetory flag if match/mismatch occurs. These actions determine how tags are selected or excluded during inventory operations(see EPC Gen2 Spec).

target.description: Specifies the session or SL (Select) flag to be used for filtering tags.  This helps in managing tag states and collisions during inventory(see EPC Gen2 Spec).

length.description: Specifies the number of bits in the tag's memory to be compared against the tagPattern.  This determines the size of the filter applied to the memory bank(see EPC Gen2 Spec).

tagMetaDataToEnable.description: Specifies which metadata fields of the tag should be reported when it is read. Each field can be enabled or disabled based on the application's requirements.

RSSI.description: Indicates whether to report the RSSI.  RSSI provides the strength of the signal received from the tag, which can be useful for determining tag proximity.

PHASE.description: Indicates whether to report the phase angle of the tag's signal.  Phase information is often used for advanced applications like tag localization or movement tracking.

SEENCOUNT.description: Indicates whether to report the number of times the tag was detected during inventory.  This helps in understanding tag visibility and read consistency over multiple scans.

CHANNEL.description: Indicates whether to report the communication channel used to read the tag.  This is useful in environments with multiple channels or frequency hopping to identify the channel of operation.

PC.description: Indicates whether to report the Protocol Control (PC) word.  The PC word contains information about the tag's memory structure and encoding, such as the length of the EPC.

XPC.description: Indicates whether to report the Extended Protocol Control (XPC) word.  XPC provides additional protocol-related information for advanced tags, such as custom memory configurations.

CRC.description: Indicates whether to report the CRC value.  CRC is used to verify the integrity of the tag's data and ensure error-free communication.

EPC.description: Indicates whether to report the EPC.  EPC is the unique identifier stored in the tag's memory, typically used for item identification.

TID.description: Indicates whether to report the TID.  TID is a factory-programmed, unique identifier for the tag, often used for authentication or anti-counterfeiting.

USER.description: Indicates whether to report the User memory bank data.  The User memory bank can store custom data defined by the application, such as additional product information.

MAC.description: Indicates whether to report the MAC address of the reader.  This is useful for identifying the specific reader that performed the tag read in networked environments.

EPCid.description:
EPCID refers to the Electronic Product Code Identifier, a unique identifier encoded on an RFID tag to identify a specific physical object.

The EPCID is a critical component in RFID systems, as it provides a globally unique identifier for items in the supply chain. It is encoded in the RFID tag's memory and is used to distinguish one item from another, even if they are of the same type or category.

The EPCID is typically represented as a hexadecimal string and follows the EPCglobal standard, which ensures interoperability across different RFID systems and organizations. This identifier can be used for tracking, inventory management, and authentication purposes.

EPCID will be reported as a hex string.

EPC.description:
The EPC (Electronic Product Code) memory bank is a section of memory on an RFID tag that stores the unique identifier for the tagged object. This identifier is used to distinguish one item from another in a supply chain or inventory system.

The EPC memory bank typically contains a globally unique identifier encoded as a hexadecimal string, following the EPCglobal standard. This standard ensures interoperability across different RFID systems and organizations. The EPC memory bank is critical for tracking, inventory management, and authentication purposes.

The data in the EPC memory bank is often used in conjunction with other memory banks, such as TID and USER, to provide comprehensive information about the tagged object. The EPC memory bank is read during the inventory process and is essential for identifying and managing items in real-time.

EPC will be reported as hex string.

TID.description:
The TID (Tag Identifier) memory bank is a section of memory on an RFID tag that contains a unique identifier assigned by the tag manufacturer. This identifier is typically immutable and is used to uniquely identify the tag regardless of the data stored in other memory banks. The TID memory bank may also include additional information about the tag, such as the manufacturer ID and model number. The data in this bank is encoded as a hexadecimal string and is often used for authentication or anti-counterfeiting purposes.

TID will be reported as hex string.

USER.description:
The "USER" memory bank in RFID tags is a user-defined memory area that can store custom data.
This memory bank is typically used for application-specific purposes, allowing users to write
and read data relevant to their use case. The data is represented as a hexadecimal string,
providing a compact and efficient format for storage and transmission. The size and structure
of the USER memory bank may vary depending on the RFID tag's specifications. It is commonly
used in scenarios such as asset tracking, inventory management, and custom identification
systems. Ensure proper handling of the data to maintain data integrity and security.

USER will be reported as hex string.

RESERVED.description:
The RESERVED memory bank is a section of memory on an RFID tag that is typically used for storing passwords or other security-related data. It may include the kill password and access password, which are used to control access to the tag and to permanently disable it, respectively. The data in this bank is encoded as a hexadecimal string and is often protected or restricted based on the tag's configuration.

RESERVED will be reported as hex string.

commandEnvelope.title: Command envelope trait
commandEnvelope.summary: Metadata shared by every command message the cloud publishes.
commandEnvelope.description:
Shared metadata for all command messages: the JSON content type and the `requestId` correlation rule.

Correlation is by the `requestId` field, echoed verbatim between request and reply. Because the command channel is QoS 1, the same `requestId` may arrive at the reader more than once for a single publish, and the reader does not suppress the repeat -- it executes every copy. Use the field to pair a reply with its request; do not rely on it to make a command safe to send twice.

responseEnvelope.description:

Correlation is by the `requestId` field, echoed verbatim between request and reply. Because the command channel is QoS 1, the same `requestId` may arrive at the reader more than once for a single publish, and the reader does not suppress the repeat -- it executes every copy. Use the field to pair a reply with its request; do not rely on it to make a command safe to send twice.

commandChannel.title: Command-channel operation trait
commandChannel.summary: The MQTT binding every command operation shares.
commandChannel.description: Every command operation is delivered on the command channel at QoS 1 with RETAIN false. QoS 1 because a lost command is indistinguishable from one the device declined to answer; RETAIN false because a retained command would be re-delivered and re-executed on every reconnect, which for `reboot` or `set_os` would be actively harmful.

tenantId.description:
First segment of every topic: the customer tenant identifier, assigned at account provisioning and stable per tenant.

**The reader prepends this itself.** It must never be written into a `mqttParams.publishTopics[].topic` or `subscribeTopics[].topic` value -- those fields take the middle segment alone. Embedding the tenant id there produces a doubled topic (`acme/acme/MGMT/clients/cmnd/<serial>/<serial>`) that nothing is subscribed to.

It is the `tenantId` member of the endpoint `configuration` object -- a sibling of `mqttParams`, not a member of it. It is first entered when 123RFID Desktop bootstraps the initial endpoint, and can be changed over the air by re-sending `config_endpoint` with an update operation.

Tenant isolation is the reason for the prefix: because every topic in the namespace sits under the tenant subtree, a broker topic ACL can scope a credential to exactly one tenant.

The maximum length is **48 characters** (per the `tenantId` description in the endpoint configuration schema); exceeding it returns status code 27 (`IOT_ERROR_INVALID_TENANTID_LENGTH`). Casing is not normalised by the device: the shipped examples send both `ZEBRA` and `zebra`.

endpointBase.description:
Middle segment of the topic: the base topic configured on the endpoint.

**This is the only segment you configure.** It is set per endpoint through `mqttParams.publishTopics[].topic` and `mqttParams.subscribeTopics[].topic`; the reader supplies the tenant id before it and its own serial after it.

The `<base>/clients/<token>` shape the enum below reflects is a **convention the source schemas follow consistently, not a contract**. A deployment is free to choose its own middle segment, and the reference test device used `MDM` as its management base rather than `MGMT`. The enum is published as the evidenced convention so that generated clients and topic ACLs have a starting point, and it mirrors the `epType` vocabulary.

Because the segment is per endpoint, a deployment can route management and control traffic on one broker or split them across brokers without changing any topic semantics. The per-endpoint limits are 3 publish topics (status code 25) and 1 subscribe topic (status code 26), which is the usual reason a deployment splits roles across several endpoints.

deviceSerialNumber.description:
Third segment of every topic: the reader hardware serial number, stable per device.

**The reader appends this itself.** Like the tenant id, it must never be written into a configured topic value.

Putting the serial in the suffix is what lets per-device commands and fleet-wide subscriptions coexist: subscribe with the MQTT single-level wildcard `+` in this position (`acme/MGMT/clients/resp/+`) to watch every reader in the tenant, or with a literal serial to watch one.

Three forms are evidenced across the sources: the bare serial (`212735201D0110`), the model-prefixed form (`RFD40-24190525100255`, which is also what the device reports as its Wi-Fi `hostname` and as `deviceSerialNo`), and a compact form in one endpoint example (`RFD400124FA`). The RFD40/RFD90 IoT API specification writes the suffix in the model-prefixed form in every topic example -- `zebra/MDM/clients/cmnd/RFD40-212735201D0053` -- which is `readerVersion.model`, a hyphen and `readerVersion.serialNumber` as `get_version` reports them, and the value the reader reports as `deviceSerialNo` in its connection-state message. Build topics with that form; use `+` at this position only to subscribe across readers.

requestIdCorrelation.description: Commands and their responses share one topic pair, so the only thing pairing a reply with its request is the `requestId` the client chose and the reader echoes back verbatim. Because the command channel is QoS 1 (at-least-once), the same `requestId` may also arrive at the reader twice; the reader executes both copies rather than suppressing the second, so a client that repeats a request must expect the work to be attempted again.

userPassword.description: MQTT CONNECT username and password, configured through `config_endpoint` as `mqttParams.username` and `mqttParams.password`. These credentials travel in the CONNECT packet in plaintext unless the connection is TLS-protected, so this scheme must be combined with TLS on any untrusted network.

clientCertificate.description: Mutual-TLS client-certificate authentication, using a certificate previously installed with `install_certificate` at `type: "mqtt"` and referenced from the endpoint's `securityParams` (`caCertificateFile`, `clientCert`, `clientKey`). The peer-verification strictness is chosen per endpoint by `verificationType`: `VERIFY_HOST_AND_PEER` verifies the broker's certificate chain and host name, and `VERIFY_NONE` disables verification and must not be used in production; for an `MQTT_TLS` endpoint the reader answers a verification type of none with response code 37 (`Invalid verification type for MQTT TLS`).
